A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MeRF study and contain readable main text and appendices. Figures, tables, equations, and relocated sections can be matched reliably across versions.

before.justification: v2 reports original MeRF and RLVR training and evaluation results on K&K logic puzzles, mathematical reasoning benchmarks, and CountDown, together with ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds results on search-based question answering, robustness controls, repeated runs, and attention analyses.

M1.justification: MeRF still inserts a natural-language reward specification into the training prompt and uses GRPO. The expanded prompt documentation and experimental variants do not establish a revision to the proposed algorithm, architecture, or optimization procedure.

E1.justification: v3 adds agentic reasoning using a search engine, evaluated on Natural Questions in Figure 13. This extends coverage from self-contained logic and arithmetic problems to factual question answering with tool use. The earlier benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Figure 11 adds a separately evaluated RLVR (Higher Temperature) control alongside ordinary RLVR and MeRF. The existing named external baselines are retained; the additional control provides a limited expansion of the comparator set.

E3.justification: v3 adds controlled evaluations varying reward density, temperature from 1 to 1.2, and prompt formulation, plus training-set correctness and attention measurements during generation of <answer> (Figures 5, 11, 12, and 14). These substantially expand the evaluation design. The original benchmark splits and shared GRPO settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained inference-prompt, entropy, pass@k, and motivation-consistency analyses, v3 adds training correctness trajectories, a temperature control, reward-density and prompt-robustness tests, repeated adverse-motivation trajectories, and attention heatmaps. Appendix A.4 also adds successful and unsuccessful response examples, substantially broadening mechanism and failure analysis.

E5.justification: v2 displays one adverse-motivation trajectory without specifying a run count. v3 Figure 10 explicitly reports three trajectories labeled run1, run2, and run3. This adds reporting of repeated runs, without establishing a general increase in runs or supplying seeds and a formal uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds difficulty-specific results for five previously studied training configurations; for example, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct has newly tabulated overall accuracies of 0.72 for RLVR and 0.83 for MeRF. Figure 13 adds Natural Questions accuracy of approximately 0.32 versus 0.39 at step 120, alongside new control and analysis findings. Shared Table 1 entries and all Table 2 math scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The GRPO objective, importance ratio, and normalized advantage in equations (1)–(3) are unchanged, moving from Appendix A.3 to A.2. No new theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations are introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about more effective reinforcement finetuning, reward–motivation consistency, and adaptation to adverse motivations. The added experiments support these claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: Section 5 refines the exploration explanation by distinguishing lower initial entropy and focused exploration from later avoidance of format-only solutions. The appendix adds interpretations concerning entropy alone being insufficient, selective attention to motivation, and suspected reward hacking. The principal mechanism account and stated static-motivation and weak-generalization limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly provides complete math and CountDown motivation prompts, including their 1/0.4/0 scoring rules. Shared implementation hyperparameters remain unchanged. Conversely, v2's statement promising code and reproduction instructions upon acceptance is absent from v3, without replacement access information. These are documentation changes, not evidence that existing experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including Natural Questions, SERL, a direct-preference-optimization survey, and traditional RL and multimodal work. The substantive positioning of MeRF as combining in-context learning with RLVR remains largely unchanged; relocating related work does not itself change that positioning.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the four-question analysis structure are retained. Related work moves from Appendix A.2 to Section 2, selected explanations and captions are revised, and appendix organization, affiliations, and acknowledgments are updated. This is a limited reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 merges the earlier Figures 1 and 3 into a six-panel Figure 1, substantially expands Table 1, and reformats Table 2 into dataset rows. It also relocates CountDown plots to the appendix, revises plot styling and prompt boxes, and adds several analytical figures and case displays.

improvement.justification: The added temperature and reward-density controls, repeated adverse-motivation trajectories, and fuller prompt specifications strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. These provide useful gains over v2. However, sparse protocol details for Natural Questions and unspecified prompt variants limit the new evidence, while removal of the code-release commitment weakens reproducibility assurances.
